newsitem.title: USA: Zinc faces bumpy ride in auto sector - Renault.
newsitem.headline: Zinc faces bumpy ride in auto sector - Renault.

text.p: The zinc industry must speed up product development in the auto industry or else be overtaken by rival materials such as aluminum and plastics, Paul Parniere, executive technical secretary at Renault, told delegates at an industry meeting here.
"You have no time. Plastics and composites are coming more rapidly than expected five to six years ago," Parniere told the American Zinc Association's annual meeting.
"The future of zinc in the car industry will be more and more difficult," Parniere added.
In Europe car makers, equipment manufacturers, galvanizers, zinc producers and associations have already teamed up to promote and secure zinc's futures in the auto industry.
"But it's not enough and we have to go further, quicker. In plastics and composites, General Electric and Dow Chemical are doing a lot of work. Time is short," Parniere said.
In autos zinc is largely used to galvanize or coat steel to rustproof car bodies. Steel still dominates volume car bodies, but the industry is changing.

Much less zinc is used in cast zinc auto parts than in the past, but the Zamak alloy is still of interest in high volume runs, though the auto industry was seeing a continuous decrease in how much of each car model was made of it, Parniere said.

In 1995 there were 20 different brands of cars in Europe, the world's biggest car market. By 2000, there will be 23 to 24 brands, cutting market share for each model and pushing down sales prices, Parniere said.
But tougher environmental regulations and demands for better equipped and quieter cars will push up costs and add weight, therefore the choice of lighter materials becomes even more critical.

The tonnage of coated steel sheets in Europe will increase more slowly in future, rising from 3.3 million tonnes in 1995, to 4 million in 1998, and 4.6 million in 2001. "The total amount of coated steel sheets will decrease in the longer term point of view," Parniere said.
To avoid this outcome, the coated steel and zinc industries must make bigger weight reductions and cut prices, Parniere said.
